tier_reason: docs/scale.md gives first-party elapsed times for the GC build and a glibc malloc/free variant of the author's GC benchmark on a dual Pentium III/500 (Linux 2.2.12, GC release from 2000), but the multi-threaded benchmark variant is not in the repo (only a link to hboehm.info) and compiler and flags are unstated, so not A; no independent measurement, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/scale.md: thread-unsafe collector 9 s vs glibc malloc/free 10.51 s (pthreads not linked), about 1.17x (derived from page data); thread-safe collector (-D GC_THREADS) 10.3 s vs glibc malloc/free 20.90 s (one thread, pthreads linked), about 2.0x (derived from page data); two clients 23.5 s vs 24.55 s, about 1.04x (derived from page data). With -D GC_THREADS -D PARALLEL_MARK -D THREAD_LOCAL_ALLOC the same page lists 1 client 10.45 s (1 marker) / 7.85 s (2 markers) and 2 clients 19.95 s / 12.3 s; against the malloc/free times that is about 2.0x for two clients with two markers (12.3 s vs 24.55 s, derived from page data), though the two-marker runs use the second CPU for marking. The page says the benchmark favors a garbage collector since most objects are small. docs/overview.md says performance is 'typically competitive' with malloc/free, that time and space overhead are 'likely to be only slightly higher' for programs written for malloc/free, that the collector may be faster for very small objects and slower for large ones, and that with thread-local allocation it 'may in some cases significantly outperform' malloc/free; no numbers there.
corrections.caveats: Only first-party numbers, from a roughly 25-year-old collector release (2000) on a dual Pentium III/500 under Linux 2.2.12 with an old glibc and LinuxThreads; compiler and flags unstated; the author says the workload favors a collector (mostly small objects). The benchmark (GCBench, C variant) is hosted on the author's site (hboehm.info, not reachable from this session) and the multi-client variant used for the table is not published, so the run cannot be reproduced from the repo. The single-thread figure is a modest 1.17x; the 2.0x figure compares a pthreads-linked malloc build, where old glibc/LinuxThreads paid locking cost; the parallel-mark rows use a second CPU for marking while malloc/free runs single-threaded. The project's own docs/overview.md describes performance as typically competitive with malloc/free with slightly higher time and space overhead (citing Detlefs, Dosser and Zorn, 'Memory Allocation Costs in Large C and C++ Programs') and slower for large objects, so the faster claim holds only for small-object-heavy workloads. A third-party 1992 technical report by Zorn (seen only as a search snippet) reports a trivial slowdown versus malloc/free with about twice the memory. License: the LICENSE file is an MIT-style permissive notice (SPDX Boehm-GC, not OSI-listed); gc_allocator.h and extra/msvc_dbg.c carry similar per-file terms, and a few GNU build files carry a modified GPL. The lead URL ivmai/bdwgc is the old home of this repository.

notes: All figures match docs/scale.md exactly; added the parallel-mark table rows and the overview's own 'typically competitive' wording, which tempers the faster claim. Usability left as copyable on the precedent of other MIT/BSD-equivalent non-OSI notices (FFTPACK, MIT-CMU); a strict OSI-only reading would make it reference, so the orchestrator may want to decide. Metadata checked: 3.5k stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-06.

tier_reason: test/libc/thread/footek_test.c is public and its comment block names the CPU (AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 7995WX, Linux 6.8) with glibc, musl and Cosmo rows, but no compiler, flags or libc versions are recorded and each row is one first-party run, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Comment block in test/libc/thread/footek_test.c, 'with posix', Linux 6.8 AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 7995WX: cosmo 40,965 us real vs glibc 111,560 us real (about 2.7x faster, derived from page data) vs musl 392,765 us real (about 9.6x faster, derived from page data); user time 47,168 us (cosmo) vs 153,985 us (glibc) vs 1,885,558 us (musl); sys time 25,398 us (cosmo) vs 2,988,121 us (glibc) vs 9,667,865 us (musl). Other rows in the same file: FreeBSD cosmo 126,803 us vs freebsd libc 219,073 us (about 1.7x); OpenBSD cosmo 138,619 us vs openbsd libc 385,431 us (about 2.8x); Windows 10 cosmo 156,382 us vs Cygwin 9,334,610 us (not native Windows locks); but Apple M2 Ultra cosmo 65,118 us vs Apple libc 45,443 us (cosmo about 1.4x slower). All ratios derived from page data.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the file (compiler, flags and glibc/musl versions unrecorded).
corrections.caveats: Results are first-party comments pasted into a test file, one run each, no compiler, flags or libc versions recorded, so tier C although the test source is public and the CPU is named. Only a single heavily contended 30-thread microbenchmark (100,000 lock/increment/unlock per thread); the timed region also includes creating and joining the 30 threads; it measures aggregate throughput only, not fairness, handoff latency or uncontended lock cost, and says nothing about other libc facilities. The win comes from Cosmo's non-Apple fast path, which calls nsync_mu_lock from third_party/nsync (Google's nsync, Apache-2.0, as modified in Cosmopolitan); on Apple Silicon Cosmo uses ulock instead and the same file shows it slower than Apple's libc. The Windows comparison is against Cygwin, not native SRWLOCK or MSVC locks. The maintainer's blog post on mutexes (justine.lol, not reachable from this session) is reported by search snippets with slightly different figures (36,905 us vs 101,353 us for glibc, and 2.75x over Windows SRWLOCK); those were not opened and are not used. Using the mutex means building with the Cosmopolitan toolchain (cosmocc) and libc; license is ISC for the core with third-party components such as nsync under Apache-2.0. The project's other speed claims (startup 400 us faster with binfmt_misc registration, README) have no baseline numbers.

notes: Every number in the record matches the footek_test.c comment block; added sys times, the nsync origin of the fast path (libc/intrin/pthread_mutex_lock.c) and that thread creation is inside the timed region. Not a duplicate of any listed project; google/nsync itself is not listed and could be a lead. Metadata checked: ISC, 21.4k stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-06.

tier_reason: bench/benchmarks-iterators-23.png and the public bench/benchmarks-iterators.cpp (Google Benchmark v1.9.1) compare lz adaptors with std::views on gcc 13.3.0, but bench/CMakeLists.txt sets no build type or optimization flags and no CPU is named, so first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks section plus bench/benchmarks-iterators-23.png, per-element column (lz vs std, i.e. time per 32-element pass divided by 32): filter 0.2263 ns vs 0.8116 ns (about 3.6x faster, derived from page data); chunks 0.2425 ns vs 0.6376 ns (about 2.6x); split_single (lz::split vs views::lazy_split on ' ') 0.3902 ns vs 0.5568 ns (about 1.4x); chunk_if 0.4922 ns vs 0.5351 ns (about 1.09x); flatten 0.7095 ns vs 0.7771 ns (about 1.10x). The split_multiple row (0.4866 ns vs 0.8532 ns) is not like-for-like: the std side passes the literal "o " to views::lazy_split, whose pattern then includes the terminating NUL and never matches (one piece instead of six), so it is excluded. Parity within about 1 to 4 percent: map 0.2384 vs 0.2374, repeat 0.2389 vs 0.2372, take_iterable 0.2397 vs 0.2378, take_iterator 0.2389 vs 0.2386, common 0.2399 vs 0.2386, pairwise 0.4477 vs 0.4602, zip2/zip3/zip4 0.4904/0.7233/0.9545 vs 0.4764/0.7238/0.9582, cartesian_product 1.1439 vs 1.1684. Slower than std: take_every 0.9186 ns vs 0.5455 ns for std::views::stride (about 1.7x slower).
corrections.workload: Google Benchmark (v1.9.1) microbenchmarks over 32-element std::arrays and a 32-character string: each timed iteration constructs the lz:: or std::views adaptor and walks it once with benchmark::DoNotOptimize on each element; the chart divides that time by 32. Built as C++23 with gcc 13.3.0.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3.0 (README); bench/CMakeLists.txt sets no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE or optimization flags and takes the standard from CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD (23 per the image name; views::chunk, chunk_by and stride need it), so the flags used are not public.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark with public code but no CPU model, no published optimization flags (bench/CMakeLists.txt sets none) and the standard library only implied (libstdc++ inferred from gcc 13.3.0), so tier C. Tiny workload: 32 elements; the filter predicate (i == 0) matches only the first element, so the 3.6x filter figure measures scanning 32 ints for one match. The README says iterable creation is excluded, but bench/benchmarks-iterators.cpp constructs both the lz and std views inside the timed loop. The split_multiple row is invalid as a comparison: std::views::lazy_split(to_split, "o ") treats the NUL terminator as part of the pattern and yields one piece while lz::split yields six (checked with g++ 13.3 -std=c++23: 1 vs 6 pieces); split_single uses a char delimiter and is like-for-like. take_every and cartesian_product iterate uninitialized arrays. Most other rows are at parity, and std::views::stride beats lz::take_every by 1.7x. Results come from a single PNG with no run-to-run variance and no comparison against range-v3. The repo was formerly MarcDirven/cpp-lazy (the lead URL) and now lives at Kaaserne/cpp-lazy. The lead's suggested category (filesystems-and-io) does not fit; this is a ranges/iterator library, filed under the new category ranges-and-views for the orchestrator to remap.

notes: All PNG numbers match the record; the split_multiple std baseline does different work (string-literal pattern includes NUL, verified with a 10-line std-only g++ 13.3 check in scratch), so that row is dropped from the claim; the 3.6x filter and 2.6x chunks rows remain the headline. README claim that view creation is excluded is contradicted by the code. Metadata checked: MIT, 365 stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-07-06; category ranges-and-views is new and needs remapping.
